entries.note: Meant loosely 'old' until about 1600, when it came to mean pre-476 antiquity; its T is unetymological, and it comes from Vulgar Latin antianus 'from before', like [[antebellum]].

entries.term: mustard in the style of the ancients
entries.translation: mustard in the style of the ancients
entries.note: French name for whole-grain mustard, from the same French word that gave [[ancient]]; Rob thinks it just means 'old-style', not Roman-style.
Like [[ancient]] and [[pageant]], it had no T in French; English added one in Middle English to match words ending in -ant/-ent.
Another word with no T in French that got an unetymological T in English, like [[ancient]] and [[parchment]].
Its T was added in French itself, the same process that gave English [[ancient]] its unetymological T; compare [[tyrant]].
Like [[peasant]], French added the final T, in the same way English added one to [[ancient]].
From Greek pyramis, which is probably Egyptian and also meant a pyramid-shaped honey cake; every pyramid, even in the Americas, is named after the Egyptian ones.
One of the few words from Egyptian; it meant the palace before the ruler, a bit like saying the [[White House]]. It was covered in their top-100 episode.
From Arabic mumia, an embalmed body; in English it first meant a medicinal substance made from bitumen or Egyptian corpses, which people ate for centuries.
From Greek sarcophagus lithos, 'flesh-eating stone', meaning limestone thought to decompose bodies; it shares [[-phage]] and the flesh root of [[sarcasm]]. It meant a carved coffin from 1705.
It shares its flesh element with [[sarcophagus]]: being sarcastic is tearing at someone's flesh.
Greek for 'little spit' or cooking skewer; it's also a dagger-like printing mark, or obelus, that dictionaries used for obsolete words, alongside the star-named [[asterisk]].
From a Greek word meaning 'squeeze, bind, embrace', after the riddling Greek Sphinx. Susan Wise Bauer suggests it may instead corrupt Egyptian [[shesep ankh]].
Egyptian name for the Sphinx statue, which Susan Wise Bauer proposes as the source of Greek [[Sphinx]]; most sources disagree.
Named after Rosetta, the French name for Rashid, where Napoleon's soldiers found it in 1799; its Greek, Demotic and hieroglyphic text helped decipher hieroglyphs.
Greek for a standing block or slab; the Rosetta Stone is a broken piece of one.
The loop around royal names that helped Champollion; a doublet of [[cartridge]], from French cartouche 'pistol charge', ultimately from Latin and Italian words for a paper roll.
An unpronounced hieroglyph showing a word's general theme, such as a scroll for writing; Rob compares drawing a gift or clock beside 'present'.
A doublet of [[cartouche]] that went from cartouche through cartage to cartridge, with an unetymological R.
According to Egyptologist Ilona Regulski, the signs should be called hieroglyphs, not hieroglyphics.
Spelling a word with pictures of things that sound like its parts, as some hieroglyphs do; for example, a bee plus a leaf for 'belief'.
A hieroglyph that stands for three consonants at once; uniliteral and biliteral signs stand for one or two. The scarab sign for [[kheper]] is an example.

entries.translation: to become, to happen, to develop, to create
entries.note: A triliteral verb written with the scarab sign, because the Egyptian word for scarab had the same three consonants.
Egyptian 'jebet' (vowels are guesswork), meaning brick, passed through Arabic to Spanish and into English from the Americas; it means the brick, its material or a building.
A Phoenician letter meaning house, which came from the Egyptian house hieroglyph and became the letter B.
A Phoenician letter meaning ox; the ox head was rotated to become the letter A, so we all 'write in ox house' with [[bet]].
A script that focuses on consonants, like Phoenician and Arabic; the name comes from the first four letters of the old Arabic letter order.
From Greek phoinix, used for Phoenicians, purple and red dyes, and date palms; it looks like, but may not be related to, [[phoenix]].
Means 'wedge-shaped', from Latin [[cuneus]] 'wedge', after the triangular marks a reed stylus makes in clay; it may be as old as writing itself.
Defined as the time before writing, when nobody could yet record what was happening.
A sign that stands for a syllable, which later cuneiform adopted.
The heartland of cuneiform, literally the area between two rivers, the Euphrates and the Tigris.
Named after King Minos, owner of the Minotaur; Arthur Evans thought the script found at Knossos recorded the Minoans' language.
